clue.text: Undertake to have lead on court?

blocks.note: first meaning: to begin work on something, to take it on
second meaning, read literally: in tennis, to be a set up on your opponent

explanation.surface: Someone agrees to take the lead in a court case.
explanation.walkthrough: The court is a tennis court, not a law court: a player one set ahead has a set in hand.
explanation.definitionFit: To set something in hand is an idiom for starting or taking on a piece of work.

clue.text: Eat away and so on, at hospital

blocks.note: etc. abbreviates et cetera, and so on
H is the map and road-sign abbreviation for hospital

explanation.surface: Eating away, and so forth, while in a hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: Acid etches metal by corroding it, wearing it away chemically to leave a design.

clue.text: Doris on shift, confined to building

indicators.note: a shift is a change of position, so the letters move around

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange, taken as written

explanation.surface: Doris, working her shift, is stuck inside the building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On shift' reads as a working shift; 'on' is part of the letters and 'shift' the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Being indoors means staying inside a house or other structure rather than out in the open.

clue.text: Feats of footballers that may need stretchers?

blocks.note: first meaning: shots or passes played with the head
second meaning: in bricklaying, bricks laid end-on, alternating with ones laid lengthways

explanation.surface: Football moves so dangerous the players need carrying off on stretchers.
explanation.walkthrough: Stretchers here are not for the injured: in brickwork, stretchers are bricks laid lengthways, alternating with ones laid crossways.
explanation.definitionFit: In football a ball struck with the forehead is one; in masonry a brick laid end-on across a wall is another.

clue.text: Knot done badly

indicators.note: something done badly is botched, so the letters end up jumbled

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange, taken as written

explanation.surface: A knot that has been tied poorly.
explanation.definitionFit: A node is a swelling or lump, as on a plant stem, where knots form; both are hard bumps.

clue.text: Ladies' magazine?

blocks.note: surface reading: a periodical published for women
setter's reading: a magazine is also a store for gunpowder, and the ladies' room is where faces are powdered

explanation.surface: A periodical published for women readers.
explanation.walkthrough: A magazine is also a store for gunpowder; the women's cloakroom is where ladies powder their faces.
explanation.definitionFit: A powdering room is a polite name for a women's cloakroom, where make-up is touched up.

clue.text: Alarming ocean perhaps uniting such a treaty

indicators.note: perhaps signals the letters only might be in this order, so they need rearranging

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange, taken as written

explanation.surface: A frightening ocean, the Atlantic, linking two nations in a pact.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Such' points back to the ocean: the Atlantic is what separates, and the treaty unites, Britain and America.
explanation.definitionFit: An Anglo-American agreement is a pact between Britain and the United States.

clue.text: Find cold anger developing in emergency settlement

indicators.note: something developing changes its form, so the preceding letters take a new shape

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange, taken as written

explanation.surface: Anger mounts at a hastily arranged compromise reached in a crisis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Settlement' suggests an agreement between parties; here it means an aircraft settling on the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: An aircraft obliged to come down unexpectedly makes an unplanned touchdown, an urgent descent to earth.

clue.text: That is the trouble with backbiters!

definitions.text: That is the trouble with backbiters!

blocks.note: surface reading: people who slander others behind their backs

blocks.clueFragment: That is the trouble with backbiters!
blocks.note: setter's reading: backbiters are the molars at the back of the mouth, and their trouble is pain

explanation.surface: A complaint about the problem with malicious gossips.
explanation.walkthrough: Backbiters normally means slanderers; read literally they are back teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Pain in a molar or other tooth is the trouble that afflicts the teeth used for chewing.

clue.text: No charge for accommodation in upper part of Hull!

blocks.note: free means costing nothing
board is lodging with meals

explanation.surface: Free lodging offered in the upper part of the city of Hull.
explanation.walkthrough: Hull, capitalised, looks like the Yorkshire port; it is a ship's hull.
explanation.definitionFit: Freeboard is the height of a ship's side between the waterline and the deck, the part of the hull above water.

clue.text: Inequality in such quotations, of course

blocks.note: first meaning: a disparity
second meaning: the prices bookmakers quote at a racecourse

explanation.surface: A literary remark about unequal quotations, which, naturally, are uneven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' looks like 'naturally' but means 'at the racecourse', where betting prices are quoted.
explanation.definitionFit: Odds describe an imbalance or difference between things, and bookmakers' quoted betting prices.

clue.text: Dog used to lead?

blocks.note: first meaning: a breed of dog
second meaning: a fighter in the ring, who throws a lead, the opening punch

explanation.surface: A dog accustomed to being walked on a leash.
explanation.walkthrough: The lead is not a leash but the leading punch in boxing; this parse is the solver's best reading, not confirmed by a published key.
explanation.definitionFit: A boxer is a medium-sized breed of German dog, and also a pugilist who fights with gloves.

clue.text: Slight legato effect

blocks.note: first meaning: an insult, a disparaging remark
second meaning: in music, notes played smoothly joined

explanation.surface: A small smoothness in a musical performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slight' reads as an adjective meaning small; it is the noun meaning an insult.
explanation.definitionFit: A slur is an aspersion or insult, and in musical notation a curved mark joining notes smoothly.

clue.text: Bachelor host gives crackers

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for bachelor, as in BA
a host is a great army

explanation.surface: An unmarried man throwing a party hands out Christmas crackers.
explanation.walkthrough: Host is the old sense of an army, as in heavenly host; crackers, British party novelties, is here slang for mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Barmy and crackers are both British slang for crazy or foolish.

clue.text: Poet's streams

blocks.note: first meaning: Robert ..., the national poet of Scotland
second meaning: Scottish word for brooks

explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is', joining the two meanings rather than marking possession.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Burns is Scotland's best-known writer of verse, and a burn is a Scottish brook.

clue.text: Mad Hatter's menaces

indicators.note: something mad is deranged, so the following letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: The menacing behaviour of the Mad Hatter from Alice in Wonderland.
explanation.walkthrough: The famous Mad Hatter makes the name look fixed, but 'Mad' is a separate instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Menaces as a plural noun are intimidating warnings of harm, the same thing as threats.

clue.text: Wise man going round America in observation-balloon

indicators.note: going round something means surrounding it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: a sage is a wise man
the usual abbreviation

explanation.surface: A wise man travels around America by balloon.
explanation.walkthrough: A sausage balloon was the elongated tethered balloon used for observation in the World Wars.
explanation.definitionFit: Tethered observation balloons were nicknamed sausages because of their long cylindrical shape.

clue.text: Given an extra handle — of silver, stated

blocks.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
to name something is to state it

explanation.surface: An object fitted with an extra handle made of silver.
explanation.walkthrough: Handle is slang for a name; an agname is an extra name added to the usual ones, a rare word.
explanation.definitionFit: An agname, like agnomen, is an additional name or epithet, so to be agnamed is to receive one.

clue.text: English flower the German left

blocks.note: der is German for the
went means departed, left

explanation.surface: An English bloom that a German left behind.
explanation.walkthrough: A flower here is something that flows, a river; the Derwent is a river in northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: The Derwent is one of several English rivers of that name, and rivers flow.

clue.text: Hybrid fruit to take in theatrical backer

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: taken as written
an angel is someone who finances a stage show

explanation.surface: A theatre investor is offered an unusual fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A tangelo is a citrus cross between a tangerine and a pomelo or grapefruit.

clue.text: Pair at tennis? It is a ladies' match!

blocks.note: first meaning, read literally: a set played by twins
second meaning: a matching cardigan and jumper worn by women

explanation.surface: A doubles pair at tennis playing in a women's match.
explanation.walkthrough: A twin-set is a woman's matching jumper and cardigan; 'match' means a matching pair, not a game.
explanation.definitionFit: A twin-set is two matching knitted garments, a sweater and cardigan, sold together for women.

clue.text: Combined charges of some other dairymen

indicators.note: some of the following words means only part of their letters is wanted

blocks.note: found running across the two words

explanation.surface: The fees charged together by a group of milk producers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charges' reads as fees; it means the animals in someone's care.
explanation.definitionFit: A herd is the whole group of cattle a herdsman looks after, his charges taken together.

clue.text: Mind if it leaves the country?

indicators.note: leaving means going away, so those letters drop out of the word

blocks.note: the country in question for a British paper
taken as written, the letters to remove

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether we would object to it emigrating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mind if' reads as 'do you object if'; Mind is the definition and if a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Brain is used loosely for intellect or mind, the organ standing for thinking ability.

clue.text: Last carriage, that is, in the rail-system

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it

blocks.note: BR is British Rail, the old national railway
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: The final coach on a train belonging to the national rail network.
explanation.walkthrough: The carriage is not a railway coach but the frame that carries a coffin, a person's last ride.
explanation.definitionFit: A bier is the stand on which a coffin is carried to the grave, the final conveyance of the dead.

clue.text: Either way, she is a showy governess

indicators.note: reading either way means the word is the same forwards and backwards

blocks.note: a girl's name, so any woman can stand for it

explanation.surface: A flamboyant governess, whichever way you look at her.
explanation.walkthrough: Showy means she belongs to a show: Anna Leonowens is the governess in the musical The King and I.
explanation.definitionFit: Anna is the English governess to the King of Siam's children in that famous musical.

clue.text: Money-changing from a bag I own

indicators.note: from means taken out of the following words, so the letters sit inside them

blocks.note: found running across the words

explanation.surface: Swapping currency out of a bag that belongs to me.
explanation.walkthrough: Agio is the fee or premium charged for exchanging one currency for another.
explanation.definitionFit: Agio is the business of currency exchange, and the charge levied on it.

clue.text: Answering call of shopkeeper?

blocks.note: surface reading: a reply, like answering the telephone
setter's reading: a signal sent from behind the shop's serving bench

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper picks up a phone call or responds to a customer's shout.
explanation.walkthrough: The shopkeeper stands behind the counter, so his signal is a counter-signal: a signal made in reply to another.
explanation.definitionFit: A countersignal is a signal given in answer to another, as a sentry's reply.

clue.text: Opening section turning into a barrier

blocks.note: first meaning: a parting, a division into sections
second meaning: a dividing wall within a room

explanation.surface: The first part of something gradually becomes an obstacle.
explanation.walkthrough: This parse is the solver's best reading; 'turning into' joins two senses of one word, the act of dividing and the wall that divides.
explanation.definitionFit: Partition means dividing something into separate parts, and also an internal wall that separates spaces.
